evals.prompt: We're about to compare two prompts for our support-reply agent. The plan is to have GPT judge each reply from 1 to 10 and ship whichever prompt scores higher. Is that good enough?
evals.expected_output: No. A single 1–10 score collapses independent qualities into one vibe number, and an uncalibrated judge with no anchors produces confident noise. Should recommend: 3–7 independent dimensions (e.g. policy correctness, completeness, tone), anchored score levels (0–3) written before looking at outputs, and quoted evidence before the label. Should reject the ~1–10 scale in favour of a small anchored scale, warn that an average hides per-case regressions and that the diff against a saved baseline is what you read, and require a held-out human-labeled sample to check judge agreement. Should flag self-preference if the judge model is the model under test.
expectations: Rejects the single 1–10 score and explains why it is not actionable
Requires multiple independent rubric dimensions with concrete anchors
Requires evidence-quoting / reasoning before the score is assigned
Requires a saved baseline and per-case diffs rather than only an average
Requires calibration against a human-labeled sample before trusting the winner, and warns about judge = model under test
Mentions that the suite needs a holdout so the comparison is not tuned away

evals.prompt: Our judge prefers whichever answer we put first. Two runs of the same 60 cases gave different winners and the order-swapped run only agrees 58% of the time. What's the fix, and how do we report the result?
evals.expected_output: Diagnose position bias: the judge is measuring ordering, not quality, so no aggregate ranking is currently trustworthy. Fixes: run both orders per case and count a win only when the same artifact wins both (disagreements are ties), blind labels to Response 1/2, offer a legitimate tie option, randomize with a recorded seed as a weaker fallback. Reporting: win rate with ties excluded and tie rate reported, or Bradley–Terry with confidence intervals when there are many variants; explicitly state that 58% order agreement is too low and that the run cannot support a winner. Note the sample-size limit — 60 cases only detects large effects — and recalibrate the judge before reusing it.
expectations: Names position bias and states that order agreement of 58% invalidates the ranking
Requires both-order judging with agreement required for a win, disagreement counted as a tie
Requires blinded labels and/or a legitimate tie option
Specifies a reporting method (win rate with tie rate, or Bradley–Terry with intervals)
States the sample-size limitation and does not declare a winner from this run
Recommends recalibrating the judge before further comparisons

evals.prompt: I want a generate → critique → revise loop for our report writer so it fixes its own mistakes. It's the same model, same conversation, and I'll let it iterate until it's happy. Where does this break?
evals.expected_output: Breaks in four places: same-context self-review defends its own errors and shares blind spots (confident factual errors will not be caught); 'until it's happy' is unbounded, so it oscillates, burns tokens, and may return a worse final iteration; generic critique produces generic revision; and revision can break format/schema without anyone noticing. Fix: fresh context or a different model for the critic, rubric-based critique requiring quoted evidence and a severity, act only on blocking findings, max 2–3 iterations, keep the highest-scoring artifact rather than the last, re-run the deterministic checks after each revision, and define a stop condition (score target or no-improvement). Should also note that executable evaluators (tests, linters, schema checks) beat model critique where available, and that a loop saturating at iteration one means the extra calls are waste.
expectations: Identifies same-context self-review as the core failure and explains why confident errors survive it
Rejects the unbounded 'until happy' loop and requires a max iteration count plus a stop condition
Requires fresh-context / different-model critique with rubric criteria and quoted evidence
Requires keeping the best-scoring artifact, not the last one
Requires re-validating format/schema after each revision
Suggests executable evaluators (tests, lint, schema) where the artifact allows it

evals.prompt: We need an eval harness for a tool-using research agent before we change its planner. What should the case format be, what runs on every PR, and how do we stop it from becoming a number we tune against?
evals.expected_output: Harness = dataset + runner + scorer. Dataset: JSONL, one case per line with stable id, level, split (tune/holdout), input, criteria, optional reference, tags, source, date added; versioned in git. Runner: pins model/version/temperature/seed/prompt hash/tool versions, caches by input+config hash, isolates failures per case, writes raw outputs verbatim, deterministic settings. Scorer: deterministic gate first (schema, required sections, executable checks) then judge only on survivors. CI tiering: level 1 on every commit (blocking), level 2–3 on PRs touching prompts/tools/routing, level 4 nightly, weekly human sample for recalibration. Gate on regressions (no case down more than one anchor, pass rate may not fall), not absolute scores. Overfitting defenses: mechanical holdout split run only at release, refresh cases from production traces, rotate saturated cases, report trajectory metrics, never tune on the reported set. Also: score the trajectory (tool calls, retries, tokens) not just the final answer, and report per-case diffs, pass rate, cost, and latency.
expectations: Defines the dataset schema with stable IDs, split, criteria, and source provenance
Requires pinned config, caching, failure isolation, and verbatim raw output storage
Requires a deterministic gate before the LLM judge
Tiers CI: cheap checks on every commit, judged levels on prompt/tool PRs, nightly full runs
Gates on regressions and pass rate rather than a single absolute score
Includes concrete overfitting defenses including a mechanical holdout and production refresh
Scores the trajectory and reports per-case diffs plus cost/latency

evals.prompt: Add a pytest unit test for this function that computes the invoice total with tax, and wire it into our CI so the build fails on regressions.
evals.expected_output: Skill must NOT activate. This is ordinary deterministic unit testing — an assert on an exact value — not LLM or agent evaluation. The agent should write the pytest case and CI wiring normally. If the agent builds a rubric, an LLM judge, or an eval harness for this, the test fails.
expectations: Does not activate the agentic-eval skill
Treats the request as a standard pytest/CI task with deterministic assertions

evals.prompt: Our RAG agent keeps returning the wrong policy document for refund questions. Can you look at the retriever and fix the chunking and embedding model?
evals.expected_output: Skill must NOT activate. This is a retrieval debugging task — chunking strategy, embedding choice, index configuration — not an evaluation-design task. The agent should inspect and fix retrieval. If it responds with a rubric, judge calibration, or eval pyramid instead of diagnosing the retriever, the test fails. (Adding an eval afterward is reasonable, but the request as asked is debugging.)
expectations: Does not activate the agentic-eval skill
Diagnoses chunking, embeddings, and index configuration rather than proposing a rubric or judge
